name: Yellowy Green
lede: Yellowy green is a vivid yellow-green from the xkcd color survey, but the phrase is older than the swatch: it is the dictionary's usual way of saying which kind of green a name means.

sections.title: A description, not a name
sections.body: ColorHub's library takes this swatch from one source, the xkcd survey, and files it as an alternate name for [[lime]], from which it is only 3.2 in ΔE away [1]. In books the phrase works differently: Paterson uses *yellowy green* to define other colors, among them pea green, moss green, ocean green, laurel, spring green and the pigment named for Paris [2]. The words say a direction, green leaning toward yellow, and not a particular paint.

sections.title: Greens that lean yellow
sections.body: Two of Paterson's yellowy greens are mixtures with a known recipe [2]. Chrome green is made by mixing chrome yellow with Prussian blue [2]. Hooker's green was first prepared from Prussian blue and gamboge, and is now more usually made from cadmium yellow and phthalo blue [2]. Sap green was originally made in medieval times from buckthorn berries, and the modern oil paint is usually a coal-tar lake [2]. Paterson also calls a young leaf's green yellowy, in the entries for leaf-green and spring green [2].

sections.title: Books disagree on how bright
sections.body: Most of the dictionary's yellowy greens are natural or pigment colors, pea green and moss green for example, and none is described as glowing [2]. The xkcd swatch is far more saturated, at chroma 91 in LCH against lightness 89 [1]. So the phrase covers a wide range, and this swatch is the brightest end of it.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The library puts the swatch at hue 116 in LCH and gives [[lime]] as its nearest name [1]. Neighbors on either side are [[chartreuse]] and [[yellow-green]] [1]. Screen colors are approximate.

origin.named_after: descriptive phrase (a green tending to yellow)
origin.first_recorded: origin undocumented; xkcd survey in the library
